moment.name: buying lifetime access
moment.confirmedLater: checkout asks for the payment itself, so a slip here costs nothing
moment.who: a first-time visitor on the pricing page

choose.name: As shipped
choose.why: For buying lifetime access, as shipped meets every standard it is held to. One press is right here: checkout asks for the payment itself, so a slip here costs nothing.

results.name: Answers the press at once
results.says: It answers the moment it is pressed, so the customer knows the button heard them.
results.principle: People need to know their action registered: the interface answers within about a tenth of a second, or the press feels lost.
sources: Nielsen Norman Group, 10 usability heuristics: #1 Visibility of system status
Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Feedback
Response time limits (Nielsen, 0.1 s feels instantaneous)

results.name: Its words stay readable in every state
results.says: Its words read clearly at every moment, including mid-gesture.
results.principle: What a button says must be readable in every state it passes through, not only at rest: mid-gesture is when people check what they are committing to.
sources: WCAG 2.2, 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
Plumber: craft/words-on-layers (words follow their ground)

results.name: It is big enough to hit
results.says: Its target is comfortably big for a finger.
results.principle: The thing you press needs room for a finger: small targets cause missed and mistaken presses.
sources: Apple Human Interface Guidelines: 44×44 pt minimum hit target
Material Design: 48×48 dp touch target
WCAG 2.2, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 24×24 CSS px

results.name: Its motion is quick and respects reduced motion
results.says: Its motion is brief, and it calms down for people who ask for reduced motion.
results.principle: Interface motion should be brief and say something; people who ask for reduced motion should get the same states without the travel.
sources: Material Design: motion duration and easing
Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Motion; Reduce Motion
WCAG 2.2, 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA)

results.name: The effort fits the stakes
results.says: One press is right here: checkout asks for the payment itself, so a slip here costs nothing.
results.principle: Consequential, hard-to-undo actions deserve a deliberate step; everyday ones should not make people work. Both too little and too much friction cost trust.
sources: Apple Human Interface Guidelines: confirm destructive or consequential actions, sparingly
Material Design: dialogs and confirmation for consequential actions
Nielsen Norman Group heuristic #5: Error prevention

results.name: You can see your progress
results.says: The fill stands out from the track, so it is always clear how far there is to go.
results.principle: A hold or a drag commits only at the end; the part done has to stand clearly apart from the part to go, or people let go too early or hold on not knowing.
sources: WCAG 2.2, 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (3:1 for the states of a control)

results.name: You can back out mid-gesture
results.says: Letting go early takes it back, so a half-meant gesture never commits.
results.principle: Starting a gesture must not commit you: letting go early, or sliding away, has to undo it.
sources: WCAG 2.2, 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation
Nielsen Norman Group heuristic #3: User control and freedom

results.name: There is a way that needs no drag
results.says: It also works from the keyboard, so nobody is shut out by the drag.
results.principle: Anything done by dragging must also be doable with a single press or the keyboard, for people who can’t drag precisely.
sources: WCAG 2.2, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA)
WCAG 2.2, 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (A)

results.name: The effort fits the stakes
results.says: It asks for a deliberate gesture before a step that asks again: checkout asks for the payment itself, so a slip here costs nothing, so the customer is made to commit twice.
results.fix: Let one press open the next step; keep the ceremony for where the commitment really happens.
results.principle: Consequential, hard-to-undo actions deserve a deliberate step; everyday ones should not make people work. Both too little and too much friction cost trust.
